title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Connect grinder function to spindle mechanics.
student: State the primary function of the disc grinder and the structural/mechanical function of the spindle within the machine.
instructor: The machine removes or finishes material with a rotating abrasive disc. The horizontal spindle supports and rotates the disc while transmitting motor torque and transverse grinding demand into its support region.

title: External Loads
student: Identify the external actions relevant to the spindle. Distinguish transmitted motor torque from the assigned transverse grinding force.
instructor: Motor power and speed establish nominal transmitted torque. The instructor-assigned transverse force acts at the effective disc/load plane and produces bending and deflection.

title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Relate the physical support region to the local model.
student: Identify the physical spindle support region and explain why the local overhung segment is represented by an equivalent fixed support plane.
instructor: The real spindle is bearing-supported. The teaching model replaces the local support/bearing interaction with an equivalent fixed plane for the overhung segment; it does not claim the real spindle is literally a bare cantilever.

title: Load Path
student: Trace (a) torque from the motor through the spindle to the disc and (b) transverse grinding force from the disc through the spindle and support region into the frame.
instructor: Torque passes from motor/drive through the spindle to the disc. Transverse force enters at the disc/load plane, bends the overhung segment, and is reacted through bearings/support and frame.

title: Critical Component and Location
student: Identify the analyzed component and the section expected to have the largest bending moment.
instructor: The horizontal disc spindle/shaft is analyzed. In the equivalent cantilever, the maximum bending moment occurs at the equivalent support/base plane.

title: Relevant Mechanical Responses
student: Identify the bending, torsional, deflection, and combined-stress responses relevant to this problem. Explain why small deflection can matter even when stress is modest.
instructor: The model includes base moment, torque, transverse tip deflection, bending normal stress, torsional shear stress, and von Mises stress. Micron-scale displacement can affect alignment and finish as a serviceability concern.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify active inputs and calculated diameter.
student: Explain the roles of P, n, F, L, E, delta_allow, d, I, and J. Distinguish editable inputs from calculated quantities.
instructor: P and n determine torque; F and L determine moment and deflection demand; E and delta_allow affect stiffness sizing. Diameter d is calculated, then determines I, J, and stresses.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
student: Draw a solid circular cantilever shaft of overhang L. Show the equivalent fixed support plane, transverse force F at the disc/load plane, transmitted torque T, diameter d, and base bending moment. Include an FBD.
instructor: A complete model shows the local overhung solid shaft, equivalent fixed plane, end force, torque, diameter, length, and fixed-end reactions/moment.

title: Modeling Assumptions
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real grinder spindle into the mechanics model.
instructor: Use steady equivalent loading, a solid circular local shaft, equivalent fixed support, concentrated transverse force, transmitted torque from P and n, small linear-elastic Euler-Bernoulli deformation, and assigned teaching inputs. Neglect the explicitly excluded bearing, geometry, fatigue, dynamic, thermal, contact, frame, and certification effects.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
student: Outline the calculation sequence from power conversion through torque, moment, stiffness sizing, section properties, stresses, sensitivities, and assessment.
instructor: Convert power and speed; calculate torque and base moment; state I and J; solve the end-load deflection equation for d; calculate section properties and stresses; evaluate +25% F and L; interpret scaling and limitations.

title: Motor Angular Speed
student: Convert shaft speed n to angular speed omega in rad/s.
instructor: omega = 2 pi n/60 = {{grinder_shaft_omega_rad_s}} rad/s.

title: Nominal Transmitted Torque
learningObjectives: Calculate torque from power and speed.
student: Convert motor power from hp to W using 745.7 W/hp, then use P = T omega to calculate nominal torque.
instructor: P = {{grinder_shaft_P_W}} W; T = {{grinder_shaft_T_Nm}} N m.

title: Shaft-Base Bending Moment
student: Calculate the maximum bending moment at the equivalent support plane.
instructor: M_base = F L = {{grinder_shaft_M_Nm}} N m.

title: Solid Circular Shaft Properties
student: Write I and J for a solid circular shaft of diameter d.
instructor: I = pi d4/64 and J = pi d4/32. At the calculated diameter, I = {{grinder_shaft_I_mm4}} mm4 and J = {{grinder_shaft_J_mm4}} mm4.

title: Deflection Relation
student: Use the cantilever end-load relation and substitute I for a solid circular shaft to express transverse deflection in terms of F, L, E, and d.
instructor: delta = F L3/(3EI) = 64 F L3/(3 pi E d4).

title: Minimum Diameter from Serviceability
learningObjectives: Solve the deflection criterion for diameter.
student: Set delta = delta_allow, solve symbolically for d_min, and calculate the theoretical minimum diameter.
instructor: d_min = [64 F L3/(3 pi E delta_allow)]1/4 = {{grinder_shaft_d_min_mm}} mm.

title: Bending Stress
student: Using d = d_min, calculate maximum bending normal stress at the shaft base.
instructor: sigma_b = 32M/(pi d3) = {{grinder_shaft_sigma_b_MPa}} MPa.

title: Torsional Shear Stress
student: Using d = d_min, calculate maximum torsional shear stress at the shaft surface.
instructor: tau_t = 16T/(pi d3) = {{grinder_shaft_tau_t_MPa}} MPa.

title: Combined Stress State
student: Calculate von Mises equivalent stress for simultaneous bending normal stress and torsional shear stress.
instructor: sigma_VM = sqrt(sigma_b2 + 3 tau_t2) = {{grinder_shaft_sigma_VM_MPa}} MPa.

title: Grinding-Force Sensitivity
student: Increase F by 25%. Recalculate base moment and required diameter and interpret the fourth-root response.
instructor: At F = {{grinder_shaft_F25_N}} N, M = {{grinder_shaft_M_F25_Nm}} N m and d_min = {{grinder_shaft_d_F25_mm}} mm, an increase of {{grinder_shaft_F25_percent}}%.

title: Overhang Sensitivity
student: Increase L by 25%. Recalculate base moment and required diameter and interpret the L^(3/4) response.
instructor: At L = {{grinder_shaft_L25_mm}} mm, M = {{grinder_shaft_M_L25_Nm}} N m and d_min = {{grinder_shaft_d_L25_mm}} mm, an increase of {{grinder_shaft_L25_percent}}%.

title: Scaling Interpretation
student: Explain the relative influence of F, L, E, and d on deflection and identify the strongest leverage in the idealized model.
instructor: {{grinder_shaft_scaling_assessment}}

title: Model Limitations
learningObjectives: Distinguish teaching result from actual design.
student: Identify important real effects omitted by the model and explain why the calculated diameter is not an actual manufacturer shaft specification.
instructor: The model excludes actual bearings/support compliance and spacing, stepped geometry, shoulders/keyways and stress concentrations, grinding-force history, disc weight, bearing reactions, fatigue, vibration/critical speed, imbalance, gyroscopic and thermal effects, contact mechanics, tolerances, and frame compliance.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
student: Summarize torque, moment, stiffness-sized diameter, resulting stresses, sensitivity trends, one mechanics-based recommendation, and important limitations. Do not claim an actual shaft size or certification.
instructor: {{grinder_shaft_assessment}}
